write.desc: This topic teaches the epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence and how to use it directly: proving convergence by finding N in scratch work and writing a clean proof, proving non-convergence by negating the definition, the first general facts (uniqueness of limits, boundedness of convergent sequences) and divergence to plus or minus infinity. The points belong together because they all work straight from the definition with the same few techniques.

points.name: What a sequence is
points.what: The learner understands a sequence as a function from the natural numbers to the reals, reads the notations (a_n), a_n and a: N -> R, and can work with sequences given by a formula (1/n, (-1)^n, n^2) or by a recursion (a_1 = 1, a_{n+1} = (a_n + 2)/2), computing and plotting early terms.
outside: the natural numbers and mathematical induction

points.name: The epsilon-N definition of convergence
points.what: The learner can state the definition a_n -> L (for every epsilon > 0 there is N such that |a_n - L| < epsilon for all n >= N), read it quantifier by quantifier, and draw it as an epsilon-band around L that the tail of the sequence enters and never leaves.
outside: reading nested quantifiers (for all, there exists) and their order
absolute value |x - y| as the distance between x and y

points.name: What N depends on, and harmless variations of the definition
points.what: The learner understands that N may depend on epsilon (but not on n), that any larger N also works, and that replacing < epsilon by <= epsilon, or epsilon by a fixed multiple such as 2 epsilon, gives an equivalent definition, so a proof may end with |a_n - L| < C epsilon.

points.name: Tails: finitely many terms do not matter
points.what: The learner can show from the definition that changing, adding or deleting finitely many terms, or shifting the index (a_{n+k} instead of a_n), does not change whether a sequence converges or what its limit is, and so can use 'eventually' arguments.

points.name: Finding N in scratch work: first examples
points.what: The learner can find N for simple sequences such as 1/n, 5/n^2 and 1/sqrt(n) by writing |a_n - L| < epsilon, solving for n, and using the Archimedean property to choose a natural number N that is large enough.
outside: the Archimedean property: for every real x there is a natural number larger than x

points.name: Writing the final proof from the scratch work
points.what: The learner can turn scratch work into a clean proof that reads in the order 'let epsilon > 0, choose N = ..., then for n >= N, |a_n - L| <= ... < epsilon', and understands why the scratch work (which runs backwards from the goal) is not itself the proof.
outside: direct proof of a 'for all ... there exists' statement: take an arbitrary element, then construct a witness

points.name: Bounding |a_n - L| by something simpler
points.what: The learner can handle rational sequences such as (3n+1)/(2n+5) -> 3/2 and (n^2+1)/(n^2-n) -> 1 by simplifying |a_n - L| and overestimating it (shrinking the denominator, enlarging the numerator, assuming n is past some threshold), then taking N as the maximum of the several thresholds needed.
outside: manipulating inequalities in an ordered field (multiplying by positives, comparing fractions)

points.name: Square roots and rationalising: sqrt(n+1) - sqrt(n)
points.what: The learner can prove limits involving square roots, such as sqrt(n+1) - sqrt(n) -> 0, by multiplying by the conjugate to get 1/(sqrt(n+1) + sqrt(n)) and bounding it by 1/(2 sqrt(n)), choosing N from the simpler bound.

points.name: Negating the definition: a_n does not converge to L
points.what: The learner can write the negation 'there exists epsilon > 0 such that for every N there is n >= N with |a_n - L| >= epsilon' and use it to prove that a given sequence does not converge to a given number, by exhibiting one bad epsilon.

points.name: Proving a sequence diverges: (-1)^n
points.what: The learner understands that a divergent sequence is one that converges to no L at all, and can prove that (-1)^n diverges by showing, for every candidate L, that epsilon = 1 (or 1/2) is a bad epsilon because consecutive terms are 2 apart.
outside: proof by contradiction or proof for an arbitrary element

points.name: Uniqueness of limits
points.what: The learner can prove that a sequence has at most one limit, using the epsilon/2 technique (choose N for epsilon/2 for each limit, take the larger N and apply the triangle inequality), which justifies writing lim a_n = L.
outside: a number x with |x| < epsilon for every epsilon > 0 is zero

points.name: Convergent sequences are bounded
points.what: The learner can prove that every convergent sequence is bounded (use epsilon = 1 to bound the tail by |L| + 1, then take the maximum with the finitely many earlier terms), and use the contrapositive to show that an unbounded sequence such as n diverges.
outside: bounded sets and sequences: upper and lower bounds

points.name: Divergence to infinity: the M-N definition
points.what: The learner can state a_n -> +infinity (for every M there is N such that a_n > M for all n >= N) and the matching definition for -infinity, and prove such statements from the definition for examples like sqrt(n), n^2 - 5n and -n^3 + n, using the same scratch-work method with M in place of epsilon.
outside: the Archimedean property: for every real x there is a natural number larger than x

points.name: Tending to infinity versus unbounded versus divergent
points.what: The learner understands that a sequence tending to plus or minus infinity does not converge (it is divergent), that unbounded does not imply tending to infinity, as (-1)^n n shows, and can prove such a sequence does not tend to infinity by negating the M-N definition.
